activity.title: I'm going to miss my cubicle 💔 Coming in, I could build agents. What this summer taught me was how to make them trustworthy. My main project drove that home: an autonomous agent that keeps AMD's ROCm AI tutorials from breaking, running them as CI jobs on MI300X Instinct GPUs and spinning up verifier and fixer sub-agents to catch failures and propose fixes. Took our pass rate from 25% to 54.5%, and taught me that the hard part of agents isn't getting them to act; it's getting them to check their own work. I also got to build a behavioral test suite & evals for a Claude Code skill that serves 50+ open-source LLMs on Instinct GPUs, and author an official ROCm AI tutorial on graph engineering with OpenClaw for multi-agent incident triage - being published on the AMD AI Developer Hub 🎉 Huge thanks to Daniel Wang for introducing me to the DevRel side, Rishi Sinha for being a really cool onboarding buddy, and Mahdi G. for the meaningful work and guidance. Last week I TA'd 6 workshops at #MicrosoftBuild 2026, helping developers run AI on AMD hardware. Our team covered ComfyUI , Lemonade, Unsloth AI , and OpenClaw running on AMD Instinct MI300X GPUs and Strix Halo laptops — and I helped with everything from setup to debugging live alongside attendees, getting developers from zero to working agents and pipelines. This year's Build was all about agentic AI, which connects directly to our team's work on ROCm, AI inference, and agentic workloads on AMD hardware. Hearing firsthand what developers are building (and where they're hitting walls) was some of the best signal I could ask for. Biggest takeaway: most developers didn't actually struggle with the models; rather, it was accessibility. Once the environment and hardware were set up right, people went from just a tutorial to a reproducible project. Grateful to my team for bringing me along. Excited to keep building at the intersection of AI and hardware. #MicrosoftBuild #AMD #ROCm #MI300X #AgenticAI #Microsoft ...more

This past weekend, we hosted the Claude Builder Club hackathon at Purdue, and it was one of the most rewarding moments of the year! We had 100 students show up ready to build, and within a few hours, they turned ideas into real, working AI-powered projects. What made it especially cool was how grounded many of the ideas were. Teams built tools specifically for Purdue: improving how students navigate campus resources, manage their time, and solve everyday friction points that most of us just accept. At the same time, other teams tackled broader problems: building for accessibility, productivity, and workflows that could impact people far beyond campus. Seeing that mix of hyper-local and widely applicable ideas was honestly the highlight. A big theme throughout was how quickly people were able to move from idea → execution using Claude . Instead of getting stuck planning, teams just built — iterating fast and ending up with things that actually worked. This hackathon felt like a reflection of what we’ve been building all year. Starting off as a small club, we’re proud to say that it’s grown into a 200+ member community at Purdue, focused on helping people go from learning about AI to actually creating with it. This event was backed by Anthropic and through their Claude Builder Ambassador program, hosted as part of the Claude Builder Club @ Purdue . Really grateful to my fellow ambassadors ( Apuroopa K. and Aryan Srivastava ) and everyone who showed up and built something. This is just the beginning 🚀 #Anthropic #AI #Purdue #Claude #hackathon #claudepartner ...more

Every app you've ever used was built for the average user. That's why you have to learn it. At the T-Mobile hackathon, I prototyped the alternative: a version of T-Life where the user journey generates itself around each request instead of being pre-built for everyone. One sentence in: "Upgrade my plan, add 2 lines, and purchase 2 iPhone 17 Pros for them." Today that's a plan comparison screen, two separate line-add flows, two device configurations, and a checkout. Assuming you already know where everything lives. In the prototype, the interface for that exact request generates itself, personalized to your account and populated with real plans and real inventory. You confirm once. It executes. How it works: the backend is exposed to an agent as tools, so the agent can do everything the app can. Three agents split the work. → Planner: sequences every action and identifies what info is still missing from you, pulling live data so the generated UI reflects what's actually available → UI Generation: renders only the interface needed to collect it → Execution: runs the actions and returns confirmation This is personalization at the interface layer. Not a personalized feed inside a fixed app, but an app that assembles itself around the person using it. A week later at Product Day, I heard CTO John Saw describe a vision where T-Life becomes each customer's own personal T-Life. Hearing the company's direction land on the exact problem I'd built for was the best possible confirmation I'd been aiming at the right thing. The hackathon was my shot at asking: what if the fix isn't a better menu, but no fixed menu at all? Demo below 👇

And just like that, my summer at Kohl's has come to an end! It's hard to fit everything I learned into just one post, but here are a few highlights: 💻 Fraud & Privacy Team: I got to work on projects across backend development, security, and platform modernization while learning what it actually looks like to build, maintain, and improve technology at the scale of a major retailer. More importantly, I got to learn from some seriously talented engineers along the way. It was fascinating to see how deeply engineering is embedded in the retail industry, from solving technical challenges to shaping the broader business and customer experience. I also saw where AI could make engineering workflows better and, just as importantly, where human judgment was still necessary. 📊 Capstone Project: I got to trade my engineering hat for a product one and work on a cross-functional project focused on retail leakage. It sat right at the intersection of technology and business, pushing me to think beyond the “how” and really consider the “why.” 💡 Think Tank: My team placed 2nd in the Kohl’s Intern Think Tank competition! We worked on a concept that digitized the in-store styling experience, letting customers visualize one piece styled in different ways and across different looks. Getting to step outside my normal technical work and build a product alongside interns from different backgrounds was one of my favorite parts of the summer. The best part of the summer, however, was definitely the people. My Fraud & Privacy team was fully remote, and I wasn’t sure what that would feel like going into the summer. Despite not sharing the same room (or state) with most of my team, I still felt connected. A sincere thank you to my manager, Carlson Quick , my coach, Donelys F. , and the rest of the Fraud & Privacy team for mentoring and challenging me this summer. A huge thank you to Trevor Hein and Coral Evans for supporting us throughout our capstone project. I also appreciated how much visibility interns had across the organization. Having leaders like our CTO, Steve Dee , show up to our presentations, ask questions, and engage with what we built made our work feel like more than just an “intern project”. And to my fellow (in-person) tech interns Megha Manjunath , Navdeep Singh , Chris Farber , Godson Ansah , and Riley Barka : it has been such a privilege learning alongside you all. From figuring things out together to hearing about what you were building, you made this summer infinitely more fun. Finally, a huge thank you to Haley Shepherd and the Early Talent team for everything that went into making this internship what it was. I came into this hoping to better understand what software engineering looks like outside the classroom, and I’m leaving with not only that, but a broader perspective on the industry and a clearer sense of the kinds of problems I want to spend my career solving. Thank you for an incredible summer, Kohl's Campus !

As my summer internship at AMD comes to an end, I’m incredibly grateful for the experience, the people, and everything I’ve learned along the way. As a Marketing Intern, I had the opportunity to take ownership of projects that gave me hands-on experience in marketing, project management, partner engagement, and cross-functional collaboration. One of the highlights of my summer was developing and executing the sponsor communications strategy for AMD’s Advancing AI event. I managed the communications timeline and weekly sponsor outreach, working across teams to ensure sponsors had the information and resources they needed leading up to the event. I also served as a project coordinator for a new partner onboarding guide, helping move the project from initial discovery through creative development and delivery. Additionally, I supported the launch of the AMD Partner Showcase, sourcing and validating assets for 64 partner listings and assisting with content review and quality assurance ahead of launch. Beyond the projects themselves, one of my favorite parts of this internship was getting to work with and learn from people across AMD. Whether collaborating with team members in different offices, asking questions, or learning more about the rapidly evolving technology industry, I was constantly surrounded by people willing to share their knowledge and help me grow. I’m leaving this summer with a much deeper understanding of how marketing operates within a global technology company, stronger communication and project management skills, and an even greater interest in the intersection of technology, business, and marketing. Thank you to everyone at AMD who invested their time in me and made this summer such a memorable experience. I’m incredibly grateful for everything I learned and excited to carry it with me into what comes next. A special thanks to Ruth Cotter , Jennifer Manning , Brittany Chestnut , Rebecca Freedman , Staci Young , Constance Wong , Audrey T., Jimmy Della , Mimi De Mass
